summary: BBN answers a recurring question: can a host computer be attached to a Terminal IMP's multi-line controller ports over serial lines? They now say yes, but warn that host connections to IMPs were assumed error-free, whereas phone lines are not, so the setup may not work as hoped.

plainLanguage.summary: A computer can connect through a Terminal IMP's multi-line controller, but the RFC warns that this interface was designed for terminals. It lacks the error protection, bandwidth and connection features a host may need.

subtitle: BBN explains the limits of connecting a computer through a Terminal IMP MLC port.

tldr.problem: People asked whether a computer could connect through a Terminal IMP's Multi-Line Controller instead of using the usual Host-IMP interface.
tldr.mechanism: BBN says this can be attempted but explains that MLC ports lack error control, offer limited bandwidth and use a command interface designed for terminals.
tldr.outcome: BBN invites real-world experience while warning that this path may not meet a host's needs.

facts.label: Usual cable distance
facts.value: Up to 30 feet, or up to 2000 feet with the Distant Host option

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 241 as Unknown and records no RFC that updates or obsoletes it. The note records BBN's response to a specific connectivity question.

sections.title: The Connection Question
sections.content:
BBN had been asked whether computers could connect to serial ports on a Terminal IMP's Multi-Line Controller (MLC). The note changes the earlier response of “Please don't” to “Sure,” while asking whether the arrangement would help as expected.

Host-IMP interfaces were assumed to be error-free, based on short or controlled shielded cables. A common-carrier line does not have the same assumption, and the Terminal IMP does not provide error control on MLC ports.
sections.plainLanguage: The MLC can be used to attach a computer, but its serial lines may introduce errors. The usual Host-IMP connection was expected to be much more reliable.

sections.title: Bandwidth and Host Features
sections.content:
The Terminal IMP has many obligations, so only a small share of its bandwidth can be offered to a host using an MLC port. The MLC command language was designed for terminals and people and provides few of the features a computer needs to use the network effectively.

For example, one MLC port can make only one pair of connections. A host generally wants several simultaneous connections and could not conveniently act as a server using the current Host-Host protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: The MLC gives a host limited network capacity and only one pair of connections. That may be too restrictive for a computer that needs to communicate with several other hosts.

sections.title: BBN's Position
sections.content:
BBN says it has no objection if someone finds the connection useful despite these limitations. The note says strong error control would require changes to the Terminal IMP and a non-trivial implementation at the remote computer.

BBN asks users to share their experience with this type of connection.
sections.plainLanguage: BBN permits people to try the setup and asks them to report what happens. The RFC does not claim that the arrangement will work well for every use.
